section.heading: 1.3 Vector Equations
section.paragraph: Important properties of linear systems can be described with the concept and notation of vectors. This section connects equations involving vectors to ordinary systems of equations. The term vector appears in a variety of mathematical and physical contexts, which we will discuss in Chapter 4, “Vector Spaces.” Until then, vector will mean an ordered list of numbers. This simple idea enables us to get to interesting and important applications as quickly as possible.
section.heading: Vectors in ℝ2
section.paragraph: A matrix with only one column is called a column vector or simply a vector. Examples of vectors with two entries are
$$\mathbf{u} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ - 1 \end{bmatrix} , \mathbf{v} = \begin{bmatrix} .2 \\ .3 \end{bmatrix} , \mathbf{w} = \begin{bmatrix} w_{1} \\ w_{2} \end{bmatrix}$$

where $$w_{1}$$ and $$w_{2}$$ are any real numbers. The set of all vectors with two entries is denoted by $$\mathbb{R}^{2}$$ (read “r-two”). The $$\mathbb{R}$$ stands for the real numbers that appear as entries in the vectors, and the exponent $$2$$ indicates that each vector contains two entries.1

Two vectors in $$\mathbb{R}^{2}$$ are equal if and only if their corresponding entries are equal. Thus $$\left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 4 \\ 7 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ and $$\left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 7 \\ 4 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ are not equal, because vectors in $$\mathbb{R}^{2}$$ are ordered pairs of real numbers.

Given two vectors $$\mathbf{u}$$ and $$\mathbf{v}$$ in $$\mathbb{R}^{2}$$ , their sum is the vector $$\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v}$$ obtained by adding corresponding entries of $$\mathbf{u}$$ and $$\mathbf{v}$$ . For example,
$$\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ - 2 \end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 5 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 + 2 \\ - 2 + 5 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix}$$

Given a vector $$\mathbf{u}$$ and a real number $$c$$ , the scalar multiple of $$\mathbf{u}$$ by $$c$$ is the vector $$c\mathbf{u}$$ obtained by multiplying each entry in $$\mathbf{u}$$ by $$c$$ . For instance,
$$\text{if} \mathbf{u} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ - 1 \end{bmatrix} \text{and} c = 5 , \text{then} c \mathbf{u} = 5 \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ - 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 15 \\ - 5 \end{bmatrix}$$
The number $$c$$ in $$c\mathbf{u}$$ is called a scalar; it is written in lightface type to distinguish it from the boldface vector $$\mathbf{u}$$ .
The operations of scalar multiplication and vector addition can be combined, as in the following example.

example.heading: Example 1
example.paragraph: Given $$\mathbf{u} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 1 \\ {- 2} \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ and $$\mathbf{v} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 2 \\ {- 5} \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ , find $$4\mathbf{u}$$ , $$( - 3)\mathbf{v}$$ , and $$4\mathbf{u} + ( - 3)\mathbf{v}$$ .
example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: $$4 \mathbf{u} = \begin{bmatrix} 4 \\ - 8 \end{bmatrix} , (- 3 ) \mathbf{v} = \begin{bmatrix} - 6 \\ 15 \end{bmatrix}$$
and

$$4 \mathbf{u} + (- 3 ) \mathbf{v} = \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}4 \\ - 8\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}- 6 \\ 15\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}- 2 \\ 7\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix}$$

Sometimes, for convenience (and also to save space), this text may write a column vector such as $$\left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 3 \\ {- 1} \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ in the form $$\left( 3 \text{, −} 1 \right)$$ . In this case, the parentheses and the comma distinguish the vector $$\left( 3 \text{, −} 1 \right)$$ from the $$1 \times 2$$ row matrix $$\left\lbrack \begin{array}{rr} 3 & {- 1} \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ , written with brackets and no comma. Thus
$$\begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ - 1 \end{bmatrix} \neq \begin{bmatrix} 3 & - 1 \end{bmatrix}$$
because the matrices have different shapes, even though they have the same entries.
section.heading: Geometric Descriptions of ℝ2
section.paragraph: Consider a rectangular coordinate system in the plane. Because each point in the plane is determined by an ordered pair of numbers, we can identify a geometric point $$\left(\right. a , b \left.\right)$$ with the column vector $$\left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} a \\ b \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ . So we may regard $$\mathbb{R}^{2}$$ as the set of all points in the plane. See Figure 1.

image.alt: A graph shows four quadrants with three points. The horizontal axis is labeled x subscript 1 and the vertical axis is labeled x subscript 2. The three points are (2, 2), (3, negative 1), and (negative 2, negative 1).

section.paragraph: The geometric visualization of a vector such as $$\left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 3 \\ {- 1} \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ is often aided by including an arrow (directed line segment) from the origin $$(0 \text{,} 0)$$ to the point $$\left( 3 \text{, −} 1 \right)$$ , as in Figure 2. In this case, the individual points along the arrow itself have no special significance.2

example.paragraph: Let $$\mathbf{u} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 3 \\ {- 1} \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ . Display the vectors $$\mathbf{u}$$ , $$2\mathbf{u}$$ , and $$- \frac{2}{3}\mathbf{u}$$ on a graph.

section.heading: Vectors in ℝ3
section.paragraph: Vectors in $$\mathbb{R}^{3}$$ are $$3 \times 1$$ column matrices with three entries. They are represented geometrically by points in a three-dimensional coordinate space, with arrows from the origin sometimes included for visual clarity. The vectors $$\mathbf{a} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 2 \\ 3 \\ 4 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ and $$2\mathbf{a}$$ are displayed in Figure 6.

image.alt: A graph depicts a vector and its scalar multiples enclosed within distinct cuboids in three-dimensional space.

section.heading: Vectors in ℝn
section.paragraph: If $$n$$ is a positive integer, $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ (read “r-n”) denotes the collection of all lists (or ordered $$n$$ -tuples) of $$n$$ real numbers, usually written as $$n \times 1$$ column matrices, such as
$$\mathbf{u} = \begin{bmatrix} u_{1} \\ u_{2} \\ \vdots \\ u_{n} \end{bmatrix}$$
The vector whose entries are all zero is called the zero vector and is denoted by $$0$$ . (The number of entries in $$0$$ will be clear from the context.)

Equality of vectors in $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ and the operations of scalar multiplication and vector addition in $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ are defined entry by entry just as in $$\mathbb{R}^{2}$$ . These operations on vectors have the following properties, which can be verified directly from the corresponding properties for real numbers. See Practice Problem 1 and Exercises 41 and 42 at the end of this section.

section.heading: Linear Combinations
section.paragraph: Given vectors $$\mathbf{v}_{1} \text{,} \mathbf{v}_{2} \text{,…,} \mathbf{v}_{p}$$ in $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ and given scalars $$c_{1} \text{,} c_{2} \text{,…,} c_{p}$$ , the vector $$\mathbf{y}$$ defined by
$$\mathbf{y} = c_{1} \mathbf{v}_{1} + \hdots + c_{p} \mathbf{v}_{p}$$

is called a linear combination of $$\mathbf{v}_{1} \text{,…,} \textbf{}\mathbf{v}_{p}$$ with weights ﻿ $$c_{1} \text{,…,} c_{p}$$ . Algebraic Property (ii) above permits us to omit parentheses when forming such a linear combination. The weights in a linear combination can be any real numbers, including zero. For example, some linear combinations of vectors $$\mathbf{v}_{1}$$ and $$\mathbf{v}_{2}$$ are
$$\sqrt{3} \mathbf{v}_{1} + \mathbf{v}_{2} , \frac{1}{2} \mathbf{v}_{1} ( = \frac{1}{2} \mathbf{v}_{1} + 0 \mathbf{v}_{2} ), \text{and} 0 ( = 0 \mathbf{v}_{1} + 0 \mathbf{v}_{2} )$$

example.heading: Example 4
example.paragraph: Figure 8 identifies selected linear combinations of $$\mathbf{v}_{1} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} {- 1} \\ 1 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ and $$\mathbf{v}_{2} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 2 \\ 1 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ . (Note that sets of parallel grid lines are drawn through integer multiples of $$\mathbf{v}_{1}$$ and $$\mathbf{v}_{2}$$ .) Estimate the linear combinations of $$\mathbf{v}_{1}$$ and $$\mathbf{v}_{2}$$ that generate the vectors $$\mathbf{u}$$ and $$\mathbf{w}$$ .

image.alt: A graph shows a linear combination of v subscript 1 and v subscript 2 with a horizontal and vertical dotted line splitting a diagonal grid into four quadrants.

figure.caption: Figure 8 Linear combinations of ﻿ v1 and ﻿ v2

example.paragraph: Click here for interactive version of Figure 8
example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: The parallelogram rule shows that $$\mathbf{u}$$ is the sum of $$3\mathbf{v}_{1}$$ and $$- 2\mathbf{v}_{2}$$ ; that is,
$$\mathbf{u} = 3 \mathbf{v}_{1} - 2 \mathbf{v}_{2}$$

This expression for $$\mathbf{u}$$ can be interpreted as instructions for traveling from the origin to $$\mathbf{u}$$ along two straight paths. First, travel 3 units in the $$\mathbf{v}_{1}$$ direction to $$3\mathbf{v}_{1}$$ , and then travel $$- 2$$ units in the $$\mathbf{v}_{2}$$ direction (parallel to the line through $$\mathbf{v}_{2}$$ and $$0$$ ). Next, although the vector $$\mathbf{w}$$ is not on a grid line, $$\mathbf{w}$$ appears to be about halfway between two pairs of grid lines, at the vertex of a parallelogram determined by $$(5/2)\mathbf{v}_{1}$$ and $$( - 1/2)\mathbf{v}_{2}$$ . (See Figure 9.) Thus a reasonable estimate for $$\mathbf{w}$$ is
$$\mathbf{w} = \frac{5}{2} \mathbf{v}_{1} - \frac{1}{2} \mathbf{v}_{2}$$

image.alt: A graph shows a horizontal and vertical dotted line splitting a diagonal grid into four quadrants.

section.paragraph: The next example connects a problem about linear combinations to the fundamental existence question studied in Sections 1.1 and 1.2.

example.heading: Example 5
example.paragraph: Let $$\mathbf{a}_{1} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 1 \\ {- 2} \\ {- 5} \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ , $$\mathbf{a}_{2} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 5 \\ 6 \end{bmatrix}$$ , and $$\mathbf{b} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 7 \\ 4 \\ {- 3} \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ . Determine whether $$\mathbf{b}$$ can be generated (or written) as a linear combination of $$\mathbf{a}_{1}$$ and $$\mathbf{a}_{2}$$ . That is, determine whether weights $$x_{1}$$ and $$x_{2}$$ exist such that
$$x_{1} \mathbf{a}_{1} + x_{2} \mathbf{a}_{2} = \mathbf{b}$$
If vector equation (1) has a solution, find it.
Click here to explore the problem geometrically
example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: Use the definitions of scalar multiplication and vector addition to rewrite the vector equation

$$x_{1} \underset{}{\left[\right. \begin{matrix}1 \\ - 2 \\ - 5\end{matrix} \left]\right.} & + & x_{2} \underset{}{\left[\right. \begin{matrix}2 \\ 5 \\ 6\end{matrix} \left]\right.} & = & \left[\right. \begin{matrix}7 \\ 4 \\ - 3\end{matrix} \left]\right. \uparrow & & \uparrow & & \uparrow \mathbf{a}_{1} & & \mathbf{a}_{2} & & \mathbf{a}_{3}$$
which is the same as
$$\begin{bmatrix} x_{1} \\ - 2 x_{1} \\ - 5 x_{1} \end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix} 2 x_{2} \\ 5 x_{2} \\ 6 x_{2} \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 7 \\ 4 \\ - 3 \end{bmatrix}$$
and
$$\begin{bmatrix} x_{1} + 2 x_{2} \\ - 2 x_{1} + 5 x_{2} \\ - 5 x_{1} + 6 x_{2} \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 7 \\ 4 \\ - 3 \end{bmatrix}$$

The vectors on the left and right sides of (2) are equal if and only if their corresponding entries are both equal. That is, $$x_{1}$$ and $$x_{2}$$ make the vector equation (1) true if and only if $$x_{1}$$ and $$x_{2}$$ satisfy the system
To solve this system, row reduce the augmented matrix of the system as follows:3

$$\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & 7 \\ - 2 & 5 & 4 \\ - 5 & 6 & - 3 \end{bmatrix} ∼ \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & 7 \\ 0 & 9 & 1 8 \\ 0 & 1 6 & 3 2 \end{bmatrix} ∼ \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & 7 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 16 & 32 \end{bmatrix} ∼ \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$$

The solution of (3) is $$x_{1} = 3$$ and $$x_{2} = 2$$ . Hence $$\mathbf{b}$$ is a linear combination of $$\mathbf{a}_{1}$$ and $$\mathbf{a}_{2}$$ , with weights $$x_{1} = 3$$ and $$x_{2} = 2$$ . That is,
$$3 \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ - 2 \\ - 5 \end{bmatrix} + 2 \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 5 \\ 6 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 7 \\ 4 \\ - 3 \end{bmatrix}$$

section.paragraph: Observe in Example 5 that the original vectors $$\mathbf{a}_{1}$$ , $$\mathbf{a}_{2}$$ , and $$\mathbf{b}$$ are the columns of the augmented matrix that we row reduced:

$$\left[\right. \begin{matrix}1 & 2 & 7 \\ - 2 & 5 & 4 \\ - 5 & 6 & - 3\end{matrix} \left]\right. \begin{matrix}\begin{matrix}\begin{matrix}\begin{matrix}\begin{matrix}\begin{matrix}\uparrow\end{matrix}\end{matrix}\end{matrix}\end{matrix}\end{matrix} & \uparrow & \uparrow \\ \textbf{a}_{1} & \textbf{a}_{2} & \textbf{b}\end{matrix}$$
For brevity, write this matrix in a way that identifies its columns—namely
$$\left[\right. \textbf{a}_{1} & \textbf{a}_{2} & \textbf{b} \left]\right.$$

It is clear how to write this augmented matrix immediately from vector equation (1), without going through the intermediate steps of Example 5. Take the vectors in the order in which they appear in (1) and put them into the columns of a matrix as in (4).

section.paragraph: One of the key ideas in linear algebra is to study the set of all vectors that can be generated or written as a linear combination of a fixed set $$\text{\{} \mathbf{v}_{1}, \text{…} \text{,} \mathbf{v}_{p} \text{\}}$$ of vectors.

note.title: Definition
note.heading: Definition
note.paragraph: If $$\mathbf{v}_{1} \text{,…,} \mathbf{v}_{p}$$ are in $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ , then the set of all linear combinations of $$\mathbf{v}_{1} \text{,…,} \mathbf{v}_{p}$$ is denoted by $$\text{Span\{} \mathbf{v}1 \text{,…,} \mathbf{v}_{p} \text{\}}$$ and is called the subset of $$\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{\mathbf{\mathit{n}}}$$ spanned by (or generated) $$\mathbf{v}_{1} \text{,…,} \mathbf{v}_{p}$$ . That is, $$\text{Span\{} \mathbf{v}_{1} \text{,…,} \mathbf{v}_{p} \text{\}}$$ is the collection of all vectors that can be written in the form

section.paragraph: Asking whether a vector $$\mathbf{b}$$ is in $$\text{Span\{} \mathbf{v}_{1} \text{,…,} \mathbf{v}_{p} \text{\}}$$ amounts to asking whether the vector equation
$$x_{1} \mathbf{v}_{1} + x_{2} \mathbf{v}_{2} + \hdots + x_{p} \mathbf{v}_{p} = \mathbf{b}$$

has a solution, or, equivalently, asking whether the linear system with augmented matrix $$\left\lbrack \begin{array}{llll} \textbf{v}_{1} & \cdots & \textbf{v}_{p} & \textbf{b} \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ has a solution.

Note that $$\text{Span\{} \mathbf{v}_{1} \text{,…,} \mathbf{v}_{p} \text{\}}$$ contains every scalar multiple of $$\mathbf{v}_{1}$$ (for example), since $$c\mathbf{v}_{1} = c\mathbf{v}_{1} + 0\mathbf{v}_{2} + \cdots + 0\mathbf{v}_{p}$$ . In particular, the zero vector must be in $$\text{Span\{} \mathbf{v}_{1} \text{,…,} \mathbf{v}_{p} \text{\}}$$ .
section.heading: A Geometric Description of Span {v} and Span {u,v}
section.paragraph: Let $$\mathbf{v}$$ be a nonzero vector in $$\mathbb{R}^{3}$$ . Then $$\text{Span} \{\mathbf{v}\}$$ is the set of all scalar multiples of $$\mathbf{v}$$ , which is the set of points on the line in $$\mathbb{R}^{3}$$ through $$\mathbf{v}$$ and $$0$$ . See Figure 10.

figure.caption: Figure 10 ﻿ Span v as a line through the origin

If $$\mathbf{u}$$ and $$\mathbf{v}$$ are nonzero vectors in $$\mathbb{R}^{3}$$ , with $$\mathbf{v}$$ not a multiple of $$\mathbf{u}$$ , then $$\text{Span\{} \mathbf{u} \text{,} \mathbf{v} \text{\}}$$ is the plane in $$\mathbb{R}^{3}$$ that contains $$\mathbf{u}$$ , $$\mathbf{v}$$ , and $$0$$ . In particular, $$\text{Span\{} \mathbf{u} \text{,} \mathbf{v} \text{\}}$$ contains the line in $$\mathbb{R}^{3}$$ through $$\mathbf{u}$$ and $$0$$ and the line through $$\mathbf{v}$$ and $$0$$ . See Figure 11.

example.heading: Example 6
example.paragraph: Let $$\mathbf{a}_{1} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ - 2 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix} ,$$ $$\mathbf{a}_{2} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 5 \\ {- 13} \\ {- 3} \end{array} \right\rbrack,$$ and $$\mathbf{b} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} {- 3} \\ 8 \\ 1 \end{array} \right\rbrack.$$ Then $$\text{Span} \{\mathbf{a}_{1} \text{,} \mathbf{a}_{2}\}$$ is a plane through the origin in $$\mathbb{R}^{3}$$ . Is $$\mathbf{b}$$ in that plane?
example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: Does the equation $$x_{1}\mathbf{a}_{1} + x_{2}\mathbf{a}_{2} = \mathbf{b}$$ have a solution? To answer this, row reduce the augmented matrix $$\left\lbrack \begin{array}{lll} \textbf{a}_{1} & \textbf{a}_{2} & \textbf{b} \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ :

$$\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 5 & - 3 \\ - 2 & - 13 & 8 \\ 3 & - 3 & 1 \end{bmatrix} ∼ \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 5 & - 3 \\ 0 & - 3 & 2 \\ 0 & - 18 & 10 \end{bmatrix} ∼ \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 5 & - 3 \\ 0 & - 3 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & - 2 \end{bmatrix}$$

The third equation is $$0 = - 2$$ , which shows that the system has no solution. The vector equation $$x_{1}\mathbf{a}_{1} + x_{2}\mathbf{a}_{2} = \mathbf{b}$$ has no solution, and so $$\mathbf{b}$$ is not in $$\text{Span\{} \mathbf{a}_{1} \text{,} \mathbf{a}_{2} \text{\}}$$ .

section.heading: Linear Combinations in Applications
section.paragraph: The final example shows how scalar multiples and linear combinations can arise when a quantity such as “cost” is broken down into several categories. The basic principle for the example concerns the cost of producing several units of an item when the cost per unit is known:
$$\left{\right. \text{number} \text{of} \text{units} \left.\right} \cdot \left{\right. \text{cost} \text{per} \text{unit} \left.\right} = \left{\right. \text{total} \text{cost} \left.\right}$$

example.heading: Example 7
example.paragraph: A company manufactures two products. For $$\$1.00$$ worth of product B, the company spends $$\$.45$$ on materials, $$\$.25$$ on labor, and $$\$.15$$ on overhead. For $$\$1.00$$ worth of product C, the company spends $$\$.40$$ on materials, $$\$.30$$ on labor, and $$\$.15$$ on overhead. Let
$$\mathbf{b} = \begin{bmatrix} .45 \\ .25 \\ .15 \end{bmatrix} \text{and} \mathbf{c} = \begin{bmatrix} .40 \\ .30 \\ .15 \end{bmatrix}$$
Then $$\mathbf{b}$$ and $$\mathbf{c}$$ represent the “costs per dollar of income” for the two products.

list.item: What economic interpretation can be given to the vector $$100 \mathbf{b} ?$$

Suppose the company wishes to manufacture $$x_{1}$$ dollars worth of product B and $$x_{2}$$ dollars worth of product C. Give a vector that describes the various costs the company will have (for materials, labor, and overhead).

example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: $$100 \mathbf{b} = 100 \begin{bmatrix} .45 \\ .25 \\ .15 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 45 \\ 25 \\ 15 \end{bmatrix}$$

list.item: The vector $$100\mathbf{b}$$ lists the various costs for producing $$\$100$$ worth of product B—namely $$\$45$$ for materials, $$\$25$$ for labor, and $$\$15$$ for overhead.

The costs of manufacturing $$x_{1}$$ dollars worth of B are given by the vector $$x_{1}\mathbf{b}$$ , and the costs of manufacturing $$x_{2}$$ dollars worth of C are given by $$x_{2}\mathbf{c}$$ . Hence the total costs for both products are given by the vector $$x_{1}\mathbf{b} + x_{2}\mathbf{c}$$ .

Complex vectors and matrices arise naturally, for example, in electrical engineering and physics.
